section.title: Job Replies to Bildad
section.sectionRationale: Job does not dispute that God is powerful and just in the abstract; he agrees entirely, and that is precisely his problem. If God is this vast and this sovereign, no mortal stands a chance in court against Him, and worse, there is no mediator to stand between them. This speech contains the book's aching cry for an arbiter, a longing that will not be answered until chapter 19 and, ultimately, until the New Testament names who that mediator is.
section.thesis: Job agrees God is overwhelmingly powerful and just, but concludes this makes it impossible for a mortal to contend with Him directly, and cries out for a mediator who could lay his hand on them both, a longing the book leaves unanswered here but will not leave unanswered forever.
section.frameNote: Six movements: God's incomparable power over creation and the impossibility of answering Him; Job's admission he could only beg for mercy, since God seems to destroy the blameless and the wicked alike; Job's longing for a mediator, since none exists between him and God; his direct plea that God stop condemning him without explanation; his meditation on being shaped by God's own hands, now seemingly turned to destroy him; and his closing lament asking why he was ever born from the womb at all.

units.label: How can a mortal be righteous before God?
units.note: the Maker of the Bear and Orion

verses.text: Then Job answered:
"Yes, I know that it is so, but how can a mortal be righteous before God?
If one wished to contend with God, he could not answer Him one time out of a thousand.
God is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has resisted Him and prospered?
He moves mountains without their knowledge and overturns them in His anger.
He shakes the earth from its place, so that its foundations tremble.
He commands the sun not to shine; He seals off the stars.
He alone stretches out the heavens and treads on the waves of the sea.
He is the Maker of the Bear and Orion, of the Pleiades and the constellations of the south.
He does great things beyond searching out, and wonders without number.
Were He to pass by me, I would not see Him; were He to move, I would not recognize Him.
If He takes away, who can stop Him? Who dares to ask Him, 'What are You doing?'
God does not restrain His anger; the helpers of {{rahab|Rahab}} cower beneath Him.

units.label: I could only beg my Judge for mercy
units.note: He destroys both the blameless and the wicked

verses.text: "How then can I answer Him or choose my arguments against Him?
For even if I were right, I could not answer. I could only beg my Judge for mercy.
If I summoned Him and He answered me, I do not believe He would listen to my voice.
For He would crush me with a tempest and multiply my wounds {{chinam|without cause}}.
He does not let me catch my breath, but overwhelms me with bitterness.
If it is a matter of strength, He is indeed mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon Him?
Even if I were righteous, my mouth would condemn me; if I were {{tam|blameless}}, it would declare me guilty.
Though I am blameless, I have no concern for myself; I despise my own life.
It is all the same, and so I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.'
When the scourge brings sudden death, He mocks the despair of the innocent.

The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; He blindfolds its judges. 
If it is not He, then who is it?

units.label: Nor is there a mediator between us
units.note: let Him remove His rod from me

verses.text: My days are swifter than a runner; they flee without seeing good.
They sweep by like boats of papyrus, like an eagle swooping down on its prey.
If I were to say, 'I will forget my complaint and change my expression and smile,'
I would still dread all my sufferings; I know that You will not acquit me.
Since I am already found guilty, why should I labor in vain?
If I should wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye,
then You would plunge me into the pit, and even my own clothes would despise me.
For He is not a man like me, that I can answer Him, that we can take each other to court.
Nor is there a {{yakach|mediator}} between us, to lay his hand upon us both.
Let Him remove His rod from me, so that His terror will no longer frighten me.
Then I would speak without fear of Him. But as it is, I am on my own.

units.label: Do not condemn me
units.note: let me know why You prosecute me

verses.text:
"I loathe my own life; I will express my complaint 
and speak in the bitterness of my soul.

I will say to God: Do not condemn me! 
Let me know why You prosecute me.

Does it please You to oppress me, to reject the work of Your hands 
and favor the schemes of the wicked?
Do You have eyes of flesh? Do You see as man sees?
Are Your days like those of a mortal, or Your years like those of a man,
that You should seek my iniquity and search out my sin,
though You know that I am not guilty, and there is no deliverance from Your hand?

units.label: Your hands shaped me
units.note: would You now return me to dust

verses.text: "Your hands shaped me and altogether formed me. Would You now turn and destroy me?
Please remember that You molded me like clay. Would You now return me to dust?
Did You not pour me out like milk, and curdle me like cheese?
You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews.
You have granted me life and loving devotion, and Your care has preserved my spirit.
Yet You concealed these things in Your heart, and I know that this was in Your mind:
If I sinned, You would take note, and would not acquit me of my iniquity.
If I am guilty, woe to me! And even if I am righteous, I cannot lift my head. I am full of shame and aware of my affliction.

Should I hold my head high, You would hunt me like a lion, 
and again display Your power against me.
You produce new witnesses against me and multiply Your anger toward me. Hardships assault me in wave after wave.

units.label: Why did You bring me from the womb?
units.note: a land of darkness and gloom

verses.text: Why then did You bring me from the womb? Oh, that I had died, and no eye had seen me!
If only I had never come to be, but had been carried from the womb to the grave.
Are my days not few? Withdraw from me, that I may have a little comfort,
before I go, never to return, to a land of darkness and gloom,

to a land of utter darkness, of deep shadow and disorder, 
where even the light is like darkness."

rahab.gloss: A mythic sea monster or chaos figure, distinct from the woman Rahab of Jericho though spelled similarly in transliteration. Job pictures even Rahab's helpers, the forces of primeval chaos, cowering beneath God's power, an image of overwhelming, uncontestable strength.

chinam.gloss: Without cause, for nothing, the same word God used of Job's suffering in 2:3. Here Job turns it back on God Himself, accusing Him of multiplying wounds without cause, showing that Job has heard and internalized the very truth the reader already knows, even as he cannot reconcile it with a God he still believes is just.

tam.gloss: Blameless, complete, the same word used of Job by the narrator and by God Himself in chapters 1 and 2. Job insists he is still tam even as he despairs, showing that his self-assessment has not wavered even though his circumstances have made that claim seem, to him, almost worthless to make.

yakach.gloss: To arbitrate, decide, or mediate between two parties. Job's cry that there is no mediator, one who could lay his hand on both God and Job, names the exact lack the whole book will leave unresolved until Job's later hope in a Redeemer, and that only the New Testament finally answers in the person of Christ, 1 Timothy 2:5.

basic.context: Job agrees with everything Bildad has said about God's power and justice in the abstract; his problem is precisely that agreement. If God moves mountains, seals the stars, and treads on the sea itself, no mortal can possibly win a case against Him, even if that mortal is innocent. Job pictures himself hopelessly outmatched in any court, unable even to be heard, and cries out for someone who could stand between himself and God as a mediator, laying a hand on them both. He then turns to address God directly, asking why the very hands that shaped him in the womb now seem turned against him, and closes wishing he had never been born at all.
basic.hermeneutics: This speech is the theological center of gravity for the whole book's ache: not a denial of God's power or justice, but a recognition that power and justice alone cannot bridge the gap between an infinite, righteous God and a finite, suffering creature without an arbiter. Job's cry for a mediator in 9:33 is not answered in this chapter; it will not be answered until chapter 19's flash of hope in a living Redeemer, and finally not until Christ, who alone can lay a hand on both God and humanity.
basic.originalLanguages: Job pictures even the helpers of rahab, the mythic chaos monster, cowering before God's unrestrained power, and he throws God's own word, chinam, without cause, back at Him, accusing Him of multiplying wounds for no reason, the same word God used to describe Job's suffering to Satan. Job insists he remains tam, blameless, even in despair, and voices the book's aching central longing for a yakach, a mediator, who does not yet exist for him.
basic.typology: Job's cry for a mediator who could lay a hand on both parties directly anticipates the office Christ alone fulfills, the one mediator between God and mankind, Himself both God and man. His complaint that God's hands both formed him and now seem to destroy him anticipates the deeper mystery of a God who both judges sin and, in Christ, bears its penalty Himself.
basic.christ: Job's unanswered longing, nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both, is the clearest prophetic ache in this section of the book. Paul will later name exactly this office filled: there is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. Job could only imagine such a figure; the gospel announces that He has come, able to lay one hand on God as truly divine and one hand on humanity as truly human, closing the very gap Job despaired of ever seeing bridged.
basic.god: God is presented here in overwhelming, even terrifying, sovereign power, moving mountains and sealing stars, a picture Job does not dispute but finds crushing rather than comforting given his circumstances. The chapter does not soften God's power to make Job's complaint easier; it lets both truths stand together, God's incomparable might and Job's honest terror before it, without resolving the tension.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Timothy 2:5 names the one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, directly answering Job's lament in 9:33; Hebrews 4:15-16 promises a high priest who sympathizes with weakness and invites bold approach to the throne of grace; Romans 8:33-34 answers Job's fear of condemnation with the assurance that no charge can stand against those in Christ.
basic.oneStory: Job's cry for a mediator is the book's deepest unanswered ache, a longing for someone able to stand between a righteous, overwhelming God and a suffering, finite creature. The whole biblical story moves toward answering that exact cry in Jesus Christ, the one mediator who lays His hand on both, closing the gap Job could only imagine.

context.literary:
These two chapters are one speech in two halves, and the halves face different directions. Chapter 9 talks about God in the third person, with a mounting catalogue of His power, and turns on the line in verse 14, How then can I answer Him. Chapter 10 talks to God in the second person, and it opens with a resolve to speak from bitterness, verse 1. The change of address is the movement of the speech. Job has argued that a trial is impossible, and then, in the same breath, he begins the trial anyway.

The first half is built on a repeating question. Verse 2 asks how a mortal can be righteous before God, and the rest of the chapter is a series of scenes in which that question fails to find an answer. There is the courtroom where one man in a thousand answers, verse 3, the wrestling match in which God is too strong, verse 19, and the washing that does not clean, verses 30 and 31. The court scene is spelled out in the language of a lawsuit, and the only figure missing is the judge who would hear both sides, which is why verse 33 is the peak of the chapter.

Chapter 10 answers the wish for a hearing with an indictment addressed to God, and its second half gathers around a line of tenderness that has been turned on its head. Verses 8 to 12 look back at the making of the body with wonder, and verses 13 to 17 announce that the wonder was a trap. Then the poem ends where the earlier speech in chapter 3 ended, with a wish not to have been born and a picture of the dark land to which he is going, verses 18 to 22. The book has now closed a circle: the first poem of grief opened the cycle, and this speech takes up the same darkness with a lawyer's precision.
context.historical:
The law court that dominates chapter 9 was a familiar institution in ancient Israel and its neighbours. Cases were heard at the city gate before elders, and a person with a grievance could bring a charge, called a rib, against another, Deuteronomy 25:1. Witnesses were needed, and Israel's law demanded more than one, Deuteronomy 19:15. The image of a mediator laying a hand on both sides draws on the world of arbitration, in which a respected third party stood between quarrelling families or clans and decided a dispute both would accept. Job wants exactly that kind of arbiter and has no one, for his opponent is the highest power in his world.

The cosmology in verses 5 to 10 is that of the ancient East. The earth has foundations and pillars, the sea is a power that must be subdued, and the sky is a tent stretched out. Rahab in verse 13 is a sea monster who belongs to the shared imagery of the region, and elsewhere in Israel's poetry God is said to have crushed Rahab as one slain, Psalm 89:10, and to have cut Rahab in pieces, Isaiah 51:9. Israel borrowed the image without adopting the myth. In Job it serves to show that even the powers people feared as gods of chaos are only helpers of a Lord who is above them.

The naming of the Bear, Orion and the Pleiades reflects the practical astronomy of shepherds and farmers, who kept their calendar by the stars. Amos names the Pleiades and Orion in the same way, when he speaks of the One who made them, Amos 5:8. And the dust to which Job says he will return in 10:9 is the ordinary horizon of every mourner in Job's age, as it had been since Genesis 3:19: the dead were laid in the ground, and beyond that the ancient world held only the dim country of Sheol.
context.canonical:
Job 9 and 10 give the Old Testament its clearest early statement of a need that the New Testament will answer in a single sentence. Job says there is no mediator to lay a hand upon both parties, Job 9:33. Elihu will speak of a messenger, one mediator in a thousand, who tells a man what is right and says, I have found his ransom, Job 33:23-24. Job himself will look up in Job 16:19 and say that his witness is in heaven and his advocate is on high, and in Job 19:25 that he knows his Redeemer lives. The line of thought runs steadily upward, from no one, to a possible messenger, to a witness in heaven, to a Redeemer.

Outside the book, the thought of an arbiter recurs in Israel's story. Moses stood between the people and God at Sinai, when the people said, Speak to us yourself and we will listen, but do not let God speak to us, or we will die, Exodus 20:19, and Paul calls the law something put in place through a mediator, Galatians 3:19. The prophets bring a hope for the one who will do what Moses could not. And the letter to the Hebrews places its answer squarely in Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, Hebrews 9:15 and 12:24.

The lament of chapter 10 also has a long echo. The wish of verse 18 never to have been born is close to Jeremiah 20:14-18, and the question Why has a place in the Psalms that are said in the dark, such as Psalm 88. And Job's words about the making of his body, Your hands shaped me, Job 10:8, are the counterpart of Psalm 139:13-16, where the same fact of being made is the ground for praise. The two passages show that the same doctrine of creation can be sung as gratitude or thrown as a question, and Scripture keeps both voices in the canon.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet wants us to see that Job's problem has moved. In the first round it was grief, and the friends have made it a theological problem. Here Job accepts that the theology of the friends is correct about God's greatness, and shows that agreeing with it does not help. If God is as great and as wise as Bildad says, then the sufferer has no standing. The author uses Job to expose an incompleteness in what the wise men of his day believed: a doctrine of God's power and justice that has no place for a person who wants a fair hearing with Him.

There is a second aim. The author allows Job to say some things that God will later call ignorance, such as the claim that God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike, verse 22, and the claim that He mocks the despair of the innocent, verse 23. The reader is meant to feel the pain that produced them, and to notice that they are said in the dark, and that they are not the last word. The poet does not clean up Job's language, because a book that pretended the sufferer always spoke wisely would be no help to sufferers.

And the cry of verse 33 is meant to make the reader ache for an answer. It leaves a gap in the argument that no human speaker in the book fills. The first hearers, who knew of Moses and the priesthood and the sacrifices, would have known what a partial mediator looked like, and would have known that even the best of them only went so far.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter records how a suffering believer speaks to God, and much of it is not a model for what a believer should say. Job accuses God of destroying the innocent along with the guilty and of hiding His justice from the earth. Those are complaints, not doctrines. The book will let God answer them, and in the end the LORD says that Job has spoken about Him accurately, Job 42:7, which cannot mean that every sentence in chapters 9 and 10 was correct. It means that Job kept speaking to God, refused to invent a false account of his own guilt, and stayed with the question, where the friends spoke about God from a distance.

So the chapter gives permission and not a script. It permits honest speech to God from the pit, the kind found in the laments of the Psalms. It also shows the limit of that speech: Job's statement that God cannot be trusted with justice is a real danger, and Job himself moves away from it when he finally sees God, Job 42:5-6. The desire for a mediator, by contrast, is prescriptive in a fuller sense, because the New Testament confirms that the longing was right and tells us where to find its answer.

debates.question: Is the mediator of Job 9:33 a prophecy of Christ, or only a wish?

views.label: A messianic prediction
views.case: Some older commentators read the passage as a direct prophecy, because it names the exact office 1 Timothy 2:5 assigns to Christ. On this view the Spirit put the words in Job's mouth before he knew what they meant.

views.label: A human wish that the book leaves unfulfilled at that point
views.case: Job says there is no mediator, and the sentence is a complaint in the negative. Read in its setting, it expresses what Job feels he lacks and does not describe any promised person. The book's own later movement, to a witness in heaven and a Redeemer, shows a progress of hope and not a finished prophecy.

views.label: A longing that Scripture later answers, without the passage being a prophecy in the strict sense
views.case: The text does not predict Christ by name, but it states, with unmatched clarity, the exact need that His mediation meets. Because God's word is unified, later revelation can honestly say that the need Job named is met in Jesus, without claiming Job understood that.

debates.bearing: It is safest to say the passage names the need and that the New Testament names the answer. That respects Job's own words and the fullness of the gospel, and it avoids reading a New Testament doctrine back into a speaker who did not have it.

debates.question: Does Job sin when he says that God destroys the blameless and the wicked alike?

views.label: Yes, it is a charge against God that the book itself corrects
views.case: Verse 22 states as a fact what the rest of the Bible denies, that God treats the righteous and the wicked alike. The LORD's later challenge, Would you really annul My judgment, Job 40:8, and Job's own retraction in 42:3 and 42:6 show that the words were at least an overstatement.

views.label: No, it is the honest cry of a man who is being tested, and God does not condemn it
views.case: God says at the end that Job spoke about Him accurately, Job 42:7, and He rebukes only the friends. The cry is not a doctrine, it is a wrenching honesty, of the same kind as Psalm 73:13, and the text presents it as a step in a process of hearing God.

debates.bearing: Both views can be held together: the words are inaccurate as theology and acceptable as prayer. That is why they belong in the Bible, and why the book does not silence Job for them.

study.originalLanguages:
Job's legal vocabulary runs through both chapters. In 9:3 the verb for contending with God belongs to the courtroom, the language of a lawsuit, and in 10:2 Job asks God to tell him why He is prosecuting him, using the same family of words for a legal case. That is the language of a man who believes the matter can be settled by evidence, and who has been given no access to the evidence. His frustration is not with power, which he freely grants, but with the closed door of the court.

In 9:8 God treads on the sea. The Hebrew says He treads on the heights of the sea, the crests of the waves, in a phrase that belongs to the language of victory. The idea of walking on the back of the defeated sea is what makes the reference to Rahab in 9:13 fit. Rahab was one of the monsters of chaos whom Israel's poets say God crushed, Psalm 89:10, Isaiah 51:9. Job claims that even the helpers of the monster cower, and he uses the image to say that if the powers of chaos do not resist, he has no chance.

In 9:17 the word chinam, without cause, is the same word God uses in 2:3 when He says Satan incited Him against Job to ruin him without cause. The reader hears the word twice, and hears that both Job and God agree on the fact, though for very different reasons. Job takes it to mean arbitrary violence. In the prologue it means that Job did nothing to deserve the calamity, and that the calamity was not a punishment. Only the reader knows both uses.

The mediator in 9:33 is one who decides or reproves, from a root that means to set matters right by argument. It appears in the same family of ideas as the word for reproof in Proverbs, and in the courts it names the one who gives a ruling between two sides. Job says there is no such person to lay a hand upon us both, a gesture of authority over each party. English speaks of a mediator; the older translations say daysman or umpire, and each catches something of the office.

In 10:12 the surprising word is chesed, loving devotion, the covenant kindness of God. Job says God granted him life and chesed, and that His care preserved his spirit. The care is the visitation of God, which can mean a gracious oversight. Then verse 13 turns: You concealed these things in Your heart. Job has decided that the kindness he received was only a mask. It is one of the most searching moments in the book, because the same words that will later appear in the Psalms as praise are used here to accuse.

The last verse gathers a set of words for darkness, among them the shadow of deep gloom, tsalmavet, the word of Psalm 23:4, and a phrase for disorder, literally without order. The picture reverses Genesis 1, where God separates light from darkness and orders the world. Sheol, for Job, is creation undone.

typology.type: The mediator who lays a hand on both, Job 9:33
typology.fulfillment: Job's picture of a third person with a hand on God and a hand on man is fulfilled in the one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 1 Timothy 2:5. Moses stood at Sinai as an imperfect mediator, Exodus 20:19, and Hebrews sets Jesus above him as the mediator of a better covenant, Hebrews 8:6 and 12:24. In the Incarnation the Son takes flesh, John 1:14, so that He can touch both sides in His own person. The type falls short in that Job's imagined umpire would stand between two parties who are equals in a dispute, whereas Christ mediates between a holy God and guilty people by bearing the penalty Himself.

typology.type: The hands that formed the man from clay, Job 10:8-9
typology.fulfillment: Job's appeal to the Potter recalls the making of man from the dust in Genesis 2:7 and the Potter and clay of Isaiah 64:8. In the New Testament the Potter's right is affirmed, Romans 9:20-21, but the deeper answer is that the Maker has entered His own creation, and has taken a body that was formed as Job's was formed, Hebrews 10:5. The dust that Job fears he will be returned to, Job 10:9, is the very dust into which the Lord of life went down, and out of which He rose. The type falls short because Job's Potter, in this speech, seems to be against him, whereas the cross shows that the Potter has taken the shattering upon Himself.

typology.type: The cry from the darkness, Job 10:18-22
typology.fulfillment: The land of darkness and deep shadow that Job dreads is the place Christ enters on the cross. From noon until three o'clock darkness fell over the land, Matthew 27:45, and He cried, My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me, Matthew 27:46, taking the first words of Psalm 22. Job asks why and gets silence; Christ asks why and the silence is the price of an answer for everyone else. The escalation is that He does not only voice the darkness, He passes through it into resurrection, Acts 2:24. The type falls short because Job's darkness is a shadow of what is to come, and Job himself will not descend into the full desolation that Christ endures.

typology.type: The clothes that even the water cannot clean, Job 9:30-31
typology.fulfillment: Job says that if he washed himself with snow and cleansed his hands with lye, God would plunge him into the pit and even his own clothes would despise him. It is a picture of the failure of any self-cleansing. Zechariah 3:3-5 shows Joshua the high priest in filthy clothes, and the angel says that his iniquity has been taken away and clothes him in rich garments. The gospel repeats it as the gift of righteousness, Isaiah 61:10 and Revelation 7:14, where the robes are washed in the blood of the Lamb. The type falls short because Job's washing is the effort of a man who has no other hope, while the robe of the gospel is given by another.

study.christ:
Job 9 and 10 lead to Christ more directly than most of the book, and the first way is through the mediator. Job's sentence, Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both, is a description of an office that does not yet exist, and the reader of the New Testament cannot read it without hearing Paul: there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, 1 Timothy 2:5. The reason Job thinks a mediator is impossible is that God is not a man like him, verse 32. The Christian answer is that God became one. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, John 1:14, and so the gap Job measured is not bridged by a third party standing halfway but by the Son who is fully God and fully man.

The second way is through the question of verse 4 in chapter 10, Do You have eyes of flesh? Do You see as man sees? Job asks whether God can understand what it is to be mortal. The answer of Hebrews is that we have a high priest who sympathizes with our weaknesses, who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin, and it says we may therefore approach the throne of grace with confidence, Hebrews 4:15-16. The reader will notice that Job's question has an answer that Job could not have given: God has eyes of flesh now.

The third way is Job's fear of the rod and the terror of God. In verse 34 he asks that God remove His rod so that he can speak without fear. Christ takes the rod. The punishment that brought us peace was on Him, Isaiah 53:5, and because it was, believers have not been given a spirit of fear but of adoption, Romans 8:15. What Job would have needed before he could speak freely is the same thing the gospel gives, an access that does not depend on the sufferer's strength.

Finally, Job's cry of dereliction, Why did You bring me from the womb, is echoed and answered in Gethsemane and Golgotha, where the Son who was made from the womb of Mary cries in the dark and is heard because of His reverence, Hebrews 5:7. We must not press this into an allegory in which Job is Christ. Job is a sinner who complains rightly and wrongly at once. But his longing for a person who can stand between him and God is answered in the one who came, and that is enough to see why the church has always read these chapters with the New Testament open beside them.
study.god:
The first thing these chapters say about God is that He is beyond opposing. The list of verses 5 to 10 is the finest hymn to divine power in the first half of the book, and Job intends it sincerely. God moves mountains without their knowing it, shakes the earth on its foundations, commands the sun, seals the stars, stretches out the heavens alone, and treads on the sea. The same praise appears in Isaiah, who says that the One who created the heavens calls out the stars by name and that not one is missing, Isaiah 40:26. Job's theology of God's power is orthodox, and the book does not correct it.

The second thing is that this power is not accessible to human measurement. Verse 11 says that if God passed by, Job would not see Him, and verse 10 says His wonders are without number. That is close to Paul's exclamation that His judgments are unsearchable and His paths beyond tracing out, Romans 11:33. The tension is that Job draws the wrong conclusion. He reasons from God's greatness to God's indifference to justice, when Scripture reasons from God's greatness to God's trustworthiness.

The third is the tenderness of God the Maker. Job's picture in 10:8 to 12 of a Potter who shaped him, poured him out, clothed him with skin and flesh, and knit him together with bones and sinews is a picture of intimate care, of the sort that Psalm 139:13-16 celebrates. Job insists that this God gave him life and covenant kindness, and it is remarkable that even in his bitterness the tenderness is still granted. The doctrine of creation is not a distant fact about the origin of the universe. It says that each person is known and shaped by God, which is the very thing that makes the sufferer's question so sharp.

The fourth is that the book holds God's freedom and God's justice together. God Himself agrees that Job was struck without cause, Job 2:3, and yet God does not say His justice is in question. In chapters 38 to 41 He will not offer Job a courtroom, He will offer Job Himself, and Job's response is to place his hand over his mouth, Job 40:4, and later to say that his eyes have seen God, Job 42:5. The God of chapters 9 and 10 is therefore both more powerful than Job dared say and more personal than Job dared hope.

For worship, these chapters teach that we may praise the greatness of God in the same breath as we bring Him our darkest questions, and that the honest question is a form of faith. Even the sufferer's accusation assumes a God who can hear.

crossReferences.note: Elihu speaks of a messenger, one mediator in a thousand, who tells a man what is right and says he has found a ransom. It stands in the same line of the book as Job's cry for a mediator and marks a step forward, since a ransom is now in view. The book keeps building toward an answer to Job 9:33.

Job says his witness is in heaven and his advocate is on high, and he longs that a man might plead with God as with a neighbor. It is the first movement past the despair of 9:33, as the wish for an umpire becomes a conviction that someone in heaven speaks for him.

I know that my Redeemer lives, Job says, and in the end He will stand upon the earth. The hope that had no name in chapter 9 now has the name of a kinsman redeemer. Read with 9:33, the two verses show the path from the absence of a mediator to the confidence that one exists.

Paul names the mediator between God and men as the man Christ Jesus. The phrase that Job could not speak, that there is someone to stand in the gap, is now stated as fact. The verse also carries the reason: the mediator must be a man, as Job saw, and must be able to speak for God.

We do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses. Job asks whether God has eyes of flesh. The letter answers that Christ was tempted in every way as we are, and invites us to come to the throne of grace with confidence, the very access Job feared he would never have.

The psalmist marvels that God knit him together in his mother's womb and saw his unformed body. Job 10:8-12 uses the same facts of a body made with care, and the difference is in the verdict. The psalm praises where Job asks, and both are placed in Scripture to show the range of honest faith.

The prophet calls on the arm of the LORD to awake as in days of old, the arm that cut Rahab in pieces and dried up the sea. It links the Rahab of Job 9:13 with the power that brought Israel through the sea, and shows that the picture Job uses to speak of God's unstoppable power is also the picture of God's saving acts.

My God, my God, why have You forsaken me, is the cry of a righteous sufferer who feels abandoned and yet still speaks to God. It gives Job's Why a home in the canon, and Jesus makes it His own on the cross, Matthew 27:46.

Jeremiah curses the day of his birth and asks why he came out of the womb to see toil and sorrow. It is the nearest parallel to Job 10:18-19 and shows that prophets and sufferers reach the same dark place. Scripture records it without softening, and God never rebukes the prophet for it.

Believers have come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. The whole scene in Hebrews 12 contrasts the terror of Sinai with the welcome of Zion, and it is the New Testament's plainest answer to the fear of God's rod and terror that Job voices in 9:34.

study.oneStory:
Job 9 and 10 sit in the space between Genesis 3 and the cross, and they say in a single speech what the Old Testament as a whole feels about that space. The dust that God shaped and breathed into in Genesis 2:7 has become dust to which man returns, Genesis 3:19, and Job pleads that his Maker will remember that He made him from clay. The relation between the Maker and the made, which was at ease in the garden, is now a courtroom in which one party cannot bring the case. That is the human situation after the fall, seen from the inside.

The cry for a mediator then runs through the rest of the story. At Sinai the people asked Moses to stand between them and God, because they could not bear His voice, Exodus 20:19, and Deuteronomy 5:5 records the same role. The priests and the sacrifices carried it through Israel's life, and the prophets stood in the gap with intercession. Each of these offices gave a part of what Job wanted, and none gave the whole, since each was sinful, or mortal, or both. The Old Testament therefore builds a need that it cannot itself meet.

The fulness of the gospel is that the need is met in a person. Christ is the mediator of a new covenant, Hebrews 9:15, the one in whom God has come near and man has been brought near. In Him, the courtroom of chapter 9 becomes a throne of grace, and the terror of God's rod is borne by the Son. The darkness of chapter 10 is entered by Him on the cross, and the light comes back on the third day.

The new creation will reverse the last picture in the speech. Job's dark land without order, where even the light is like darkness, is answered by a city that has no need of sun or moon, since the glory of God gives it light, Revelation 21:23, and where there will be no more night, Revelation 22:5. The God whom Job could not see when He passed by, Job 9:11, will be seen face to face, Revelation 22:4. What Job asked for in the dark, a fair hearing and a hand laid on both sides, is given at the end as a home.

quiz.q: Why does Job say a mortal cannot be righteous before God (9:2-3)?

options.text: Because God's power and wisdom are so overwhelming that a mortal could not answer Him even one time out of a thousand.
options.note: Job's whole argument in this section builds on the sheer scale of God's power described in the following verses.

options.text: Because God moves mountains and shakes the earth, a power far beyond anything a mortal could resist or contend with.
options.note: A true supporting detail from the passage, though less precise than Job's direct statement about the impossibility of answering God even once in a thousand times.

options.text: Because his friends have finally convinced him of his guilt.
options.note: Job explicitly rejects his friends' arguments; his despair here is about the nature of standing before God, not agreement with the friends.

options.text: Because Job believes he has actually committed some specific hidden sin.
options.note: Job maintains his innocence throughout; his point is about the impossibility of contending with God, not a confession of guilt.

quiz.q: What does Job long for in 9:33 that does not yet exist for him?

options.text: A mediator who could lay his hand on both God and himself.
options.note: This is the exact wording of Job's lament, a longing the New Testament will later answer in Christ, 1 Timothy 2:5.

options.text: Someone able to arbitrate his case fairly before God, since he is not a man like God whom he could simply answer.
options.note: Captures the substance of Job's longing, though less precise than the exact image of a mediator laying a hand on both parties.

options.text: A written record of his good deeds.
options.note: Job does long to be heard and vindicated, which will surface later in chapter 19, but the specific longing named in 9:33 is for a mediator, not a written record.

options.text: A larger inheritance for his descendants.
options.note: Job's longing here is specifically for an arbiter between himself and God, not for material inheritance.

quiz.q: What troubling claim does Job make in 9:22, and how should it be read?

options.text: That God destroys both the blameless and the wicked alike; it is an honest but raw observation from a man in anguish, not a settled doctrinal statement.
options.note: The chapter presents this as Job's grieving attempt to make sense of what he observes, within a speech that still appeals to God as Judge.

options.text: That outcomes in this life do not reliably distinguish between the righteous and the wicked.
options.note: A true summary of Job's underlying observation, though less pointed than his own raw wording that God destroys both alike.

options.text: That Job has proof of a specific instance where God acted wrongly.
options.note: Job offers this as a general, pained observation rather than a specific proven case.

options.text: That God has abandoned the world to chaos with no ongoing involvement.
options.note: Job's whole speech assumes God's active, powerful involvement in the world; his complaint is that this involvement feels unjust, not absent.

quiz.q: In chapter 10, what does Job appeal to about his own origin?

options.text: That God's own hands shaped and formed him in the womb, making it seem contradictory that those same hands would now seem turned to destroy him.
options.note: Verses 8-12 develop this meditation on divine craftsmanship now apparently working against its own creation.

options.text: That God clothed him with skin and flesh and granted him life, care that now seems reversed in his present affliction.
options.note: A true detail from Job's meditation, though less complete than the full contrast between careful creation and apparent destruction.

options.text: That his birth was entirely random and outside God's involvement.
options.note: Job's whole point is the opposite: God was intimately, deliberately involved in forming him, which is what makes his current suffering feel so contradictory.

options.text: That his parents were responsible for his current suffering.
options.note: Job's appeal in this chapter is to God as his maker, not to any human parent.

quiz.q: How does this speech's cry for a mediator connect to the rest of Scripture?

options.text: It anticipates 1 Timothy 2:5's declaration that there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who can lay a hand on both parties as Job longed for.
options.note: This connection is one of the clearest typological threads running from Job through to the New Testament's doctrine of Christ's mediatorial office.

options.text: It points forward to a figure who could represent humanity fully before God, later revealed more clearly in the New Testament.
options.note: Correct in its general direction, though less precise than naming 1 Timothy 2:5's specific answer of Christ as the one mediator.

options.text: It is fulfilled by the priesthood of Aaron established later in Exodus.
options.note: The Aaronic priesthood offers partial mediation through sacrifice, but Job's specific longing, one who can lay a hand on both God and man as equal parties, is uniquely fulfilled in the God-man, Christ.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to any later biblical teaching.
options.note: The New Testament's teaching on Christ's mediatorial role directly answers this exact longing voiced in Job 9:33.

questions: Job agrees God is powerful and just, and that very agreement deepens his despair rather than resolving it. Has believing something true about God ever felt harder to bear than comforting, and how did you sit with that tension?
Job cries out for a mediator who does not yet exist for him. How does knowing that Christ is exactly that mediator change the way you bring your own hardest complaints before God?

Job accuses God of multiplying his wounds without cause, using God's own word back against Him. Have you ever found yourself arguing with God using truths you actually believe, and what did that reveal about your faith?

Job meditates on being formed by God's own hands, now seemingly turned against him. Where do you find it hard to reconcile God's intimate care in shaping your life with the pain you are currently experiencing?

This speech ends without resolution, in a longing for darkness and rest. What helps you keep bringing unresolved pain back to God in prayer, rather than either denying it or giving up on Him entirely?

translationNotes.note: The helpers of Rahab refers to a mythic chaos monster tradition, distinct from the woman Rahab of Jericho; the image conveys forces of untamed chaos submitting entirely to God's power.

Without cause renders chinam, the same word God used in 2:3 to describe Job's undeserved suffering; Job here turns the word back toward God as an accusation, showing he has absorbed the very truth the reader already knows.

Mediator renders yakach, meaning one who arbitrates or decides between two parties; this verse is widely recognized as an Old Testament anticipation of the mediatorial office fulfilled in Christ, 1 Timothy 2:5.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture toolkit for Job 9:1-10:22. no other substantive changes were made to the verse text.
